meta.reportLabel: The AI-capex scare is now the second force on this board: the Nasdaq 100 is in correction, gold had its worst month since 2008 and December Fed pricing has slipped from 80% to near 72%.
meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: For months this file has had one correlated risk, the Middle East energy shock, and every hawkish repricing on the board traced back to it. A second force has now arrived from the opposite direction: the Nasdaq 100 is more than 10% below its October 6 high in its third correction of 2026 on doubts about whether AI capital spending earns its return, and that is draining the hike premium the oil shock built. Gold has just had its worst month since 2008, silver is minus 19.29% on the month, copper is minus 2.73% today and December Fed pricing has fallen from about 80% a week ago to roughly 72% - yet DXY is 101.739 and minus 0.04%, so FX has not priced any of it.

update.title: 🇳🇿 NZD analysis updated
update.text: Q3 unemployment 5.7% vs 5.5% forecast and employment minus 0.1% vs plus 0.4%, with Q2 revised to 0.3%. Score cut to minus 2; EUR/NZD through 2.00.

meta.nextBigEvent: The Bank of England on Thursday November 5 at 12:00Z with the Monetary Policy Report, where ForexFactory carries a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold and pricing sits at 93.5% to 94%, with Bailey following at 12:30Z. Before that the US votes today at 15:16Z and New Zealand Q3 employment lands at 21:45Z; US and Canadian payrolls print together Friday 13:30Z and New Zealand votes Saturday.

dailyRead: Start with what is genuinely new, because it is not the oil story this file has led with for weeks. The AI-capital-spending trade has cracked, and it is draining the hawkish premium out of this board from the side nobody was watching. The Nasdaq 100 closed Monday more than 10% below its October 6 high, its third technical correction of 2026, on spreading doubt about whether AI capex earns a return and on the wave of debt the hyperscalers are issuing to fund it - Oracle alone is raising $20 billion in stock and bonds. The damage is showing up in exactly the places that matter here. Gold is 3920.33 and minus 0.68%, minus 3.44% on the week and minus 5.30% on the month after its worst month since 2008, and the cause was not a haven unwind but forced liquidation: when the Nasdaq fell, leveraged books sold the liquid thing, and gold is the liquid thing. Silver is worse at 49.279, minus 2.71% today, minus 9.43% on the week and minus 19.29% on the month, which takes the gold-silver ratio to 79.55 from 77.77 yesterday. Copper is 6.3646 and minus 2.73%. And the front end has noticed: CME FedWatch pricing for a December 9 hike has slipped to roughly 71% to 74% from about 80% a week ago, with analysts naming the AI investment slowdown as the reason. Here is the part that is not obvious and that is the trade. Three of the eight central banks on this board named AI demand, explicitly, as a reason they are tightening. The RBA's statement this morning cited AI-related demand for technology goods alongside fuel and capacity constraints. Ueda told parliament on October 30 that strong global AI demand was adding to price pressures on top of a tight labour market. The RBNZ's October minutes attributed part of the rise in global yields to demand for capital to support AI investment. If that demand impulse is what is now being repriced, then the hawkish case for the Australian dollar, the yen and the kiwi is being attacked from a second direction at the same time the oil premium deflates - and copper, minus 3.96% on the week, is the cleanest real-time read on it. None of this is in spot. DXY is 101.739 and minus 0.04%. That gap is today's opportunity. Second, the oil story, which has stalled rather than resolved. WTI is 97.301 and plus 0.87%, Brent 105.762 and plus 0.95%, a modest bounce after Monday's drop of more than 6%. Araghchi's two-day plan - US measures on day one, the Strait reopening on day two, cut down from seven days by Qatari mediation - is still an Iranian offer conditioned on Washington accepting a long list: lifting the sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum collapsed in July, restoring the June oil waivers, shrinking the US military presence, recognising Iran-and-Oman-designated shipping routes and releasing frozen funds. Washington has neither accepted nor rejected it publicly, and Trump has warned that US targets remain. Reports that the US has indicated readiness to accept are attributed to Al Jazeera and are not confirmed, and this file will not trade them. OPEC+ left December output targets unchanged. So crude is a headline binary in both directions, still plus 8.80% on the month and plus 69.46% on the year, and the physical constraint has not changed. Third, sterling, which keeps the board outright and is the one currency whose case does not depend on either of the above. The Bank of England votes Thursday at 12:00Z with the Monetary Policy Report: ForexFactory carries a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold, pricing runs 93.5% to 94%, and the data supports it - CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 and wage growth 3.7%. GBP/USD is 1.34108 and plus 1.43% on the month, and the TradingEconomics path is 4.00% in Q4/26 then 4.25% from Q1/27, so Thursday is the first of two rather than the terminal move. The invalidation is unchanged and dated: a Monetary Policy Report that caps the path at 4.00%, and Bailey at 12:30Z. Fourth, the havens, where one works and one does not. The franc comes up from zero to plus one, and the evidence is a month rather than a day: USD/CHF is 0.81802 and minus 1.51% on the month, EUR/CHF 0.91563 and minus 1.77%, CHF/JPY 192.936 and plus 1.47%. Through a genuine global de-risking episode - an equity correction that liquidated gold - the franc strengthened against the dollar, the euro and the yen, which is precisely what a haven is supposed to do and precisely what gold failed to do. The yen did not. USD/JPY is 157.835 and minus 0.07%, pinned just under 158 not by demand for yen but by Finance Minister Katayama's warning that the joint FX statement with the United States stands and Tokyo will act against disorderly moves. That is the third time in a week the yen has had a reason to rally and refused. The forward case is intact - the BoJ held 1.25% on an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for a faster move to 1.5%, December 18 is priced at 75% to 80%, and the Bank lifted its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% - but a forward case that spot has declined three times is a position to size down, not up. The clean expression of both facts in one ticket is long CHF/JPY. Fifth, the binaries, of which there are four inside five days. America votes today at 15:16Z and the shape has hardened rather than loosened: Kalshi and Polymarket now put a Democratic sweep at 74% to 78% against roughly 71% yesterday, with the House at 94% safe and the Senate near 74%. A priced base case means the tail is where the move is. New Zealand prints Q3 employment tonight at 21:45Z, unemployment forecast 5.5% from 5.6% with employment up 0.4%, and then votes Saturday with Labour pledging to restore the RBNZ's dual mandate - though Westpac makes the useful point that the December 9 meeting proceeds under the current mandate whatever the result, so the institutional discount is a February story and not a December one. That is a refinement of yesterday's call, not a reversal: the kiwi stays at the bottom on timing risk after a 4-3 refusal to deliver a hike priced near 90%, not on its path, which remains the steepest on this board at 2.75% rising toward 4.00% by Q3/27. Australia delivered 4.85% this morning on a 6-3 vote, the highest cash rate since late 2008 and the fifth hike this year, and Bullock then declined to guide at all; it keeps plus one on the rate and loses the direction, and copper now undercuts the AI leg of its own inflation case. Canada stays at plus one and is quietly validated: USD/CAD is 1.39701 and minus 0.12% as crude bounces, which is the move this file said yesterday was missing from the currency, though December 9 remains a coin flip and jobs print Friday against a plus 14.6k forecast after September's minus 68,300. The cleanest trades are unchanged in direction and clearer in reason: the three-point gap GBP/NZD long, AUD/NZD long and EUR/NZD long, with the new idea being long CHF/JPY and short silver against gold rather than either outright.

today.headline: Q3 labour missed on every measure - unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast, employment minus 0.1% against plus 0.4% - and the kiwi lost 0.52%.
today.read: This file named tonight's print the first of two dated repair points for the weakest currency on the board, and it broke in the other direction. Unemployment is 5.7% from 5.6%, above the 5.5% consensus and the highest since 2016; employment fell 0.1% on the quarter against a plus 0.4% forecast, and Q2 was revised down to plus 0.3% from plus 0.5%, so the starting point was softer too. Participation dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, which means joblessness rose even as people left the workforce, and private-sector wages ex overtime slowed to 2.0% year over year from 2.1% - the wage channel the hawks need is cooling. NZD/USD is 0.55857 and minus 0.52%, minus 1.69% on the week; EUR/NZD has traded through 2.00 to 2.00305 and plus 0.56%, GBP/NZD 2.40157 and plus 0.70%, NZD/CAD 0.78254 and minus 0.36%, NZD/CHF 0.45854 and minus 0.27%. The score goes to minus 2 on a specific dated test this file set and the data failed, not on noise. December 9 is still the base case rather than a hold - the October hold was 4-3 with members agreeing more tightening would likely be needed, Breman said the chance of a December move is high, and TradingEconomics keeps 3.00% - but the two-sidedness is now real and Westpac itself calls the hike not a done deal. Pricing was 77% to 80% before the print and a verified post-print figure is not yet available; front-end swaps are the market to watch. Saturday's election is the only repair point left before December 9.

today.headline: The RBA delivered 4.85% on a 6-3 vote, the highest cash rate since late 2008, and the Australian dollar is lower across the board rather than higher.
today.read: The hike was owned before it landed and the press conference removed what was left: Bullock declined to put anything in place of the deleted tightening pledge. What is new today is that the statement's own reasoning is being undermined in real time. The RBA named AI-related demand for technology goods alongside fuel and capacity constraints as the source of broad-based price pressure, and copper - the cleanest market read on that demand - is 6.3646 and minus 2.73%, minus 3.96% on the week. AUD/USD is 0.69805 and minus 0.27%, AUD/NZD minus 0.47%, AUD/CAD minus 0.38%, AUD/CHF minus 0.34%. Australia keeps the highest policy rate on the board, which holds the score at plus one, but it now has no guidance and a weakening commodity leg beneath its inflation case. September employment at minus 39,300 with unemployment at 4.7% and rising is the domestic counterweight. December 8 is a hold; February is the meeting to trade, and the minutes on November 17 are the next read.

today.headline: December hike pricing slipped to roughly 71% to 74% from about 80% a week ago on the AI investment scare, and America votes at 15:16Z.
today.read: This is the day's most important repricing and it is happening in rates rather than in spot: DXY is 101.739 and minus 0.04%, essentially unchanged, while the December 9 hike that underwrites the dollar has lost nearly ten points of probability. The cause is not the inflation data, which is still hot - CPI 3.7% in September and PPI 6.3% year over year, the fastest since December 2022 - but the Nasdaq 100's third correction of 2026 and the doubt it casts on the AI capital-spending cycle. The Fed held on October 28 by 10-2 with two dissents for a hike, so the committee's hawkish wing is intact; what has changed is the market's confidence that growth will let them act. Today's midterms are the nearer binary, with a Democratic sweep at 74% to 78% on Kalshi and Polymarket against roughly 71% yesterday, the House 94% safe and the Senate near 74%. A hardened base case means the move lives in the tail. Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast after September's 29,000 is the data that settles December.

today.headline: Crude bounced and the Canadian dollar firmed with it, closing part of the gap this file flagged yesterday as the board's clearest mispricing.
today.read: USD/CAD is 1.39701 and minus 0.12% with WTI at 97.301 and plus 0.87%. Yesterday this file said the currency had not moved on a three-and-a-half percent fall in crude and that the gap was the cleanest mispricing on the board; the currency has now started to follow, which validates the direction without resolving the December question. That question is still genuinely open. The Bank hiked to 2.50% on October 28 for the first time in three years and projects CPI averaging 3% in 2027, a full point above July, but Macklem said there is no predetermined path, National Bank put December near 50%, and new US tariffs follow the breakdown of trade talks. Core inflation at 2.2% is the softest on this board outside Switzerland and Japan. Friday's employment print at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast, after September's minus 68,300, is the single biggest input into December 9.

today.headline: The franc barely moved today but comes up to plus one, because it is the only haven that worked through an equity correction that liquidated gold.
today.read: The upgrade rests on a month, not a session, which is why it is not a flip on noise. USD/CHF is 0.81802 and minus 1.51% on the month, EUR/CHF 0.91563 and minus 1.77%, CHF/JPY 192.936 and plus 1.47%. Over the stretch in which the Nasdaq 100 fell into its third correction of the year and gold recorded its worst month since 2008, the franc gained against the dollar, the euro and the yen - the textbook behaviour that gold and the yen both failed to deliver. The cap is policy: the SNB is at 0.00%, held on September 24, and December 10 is a hold, so this is a relative-safety bid rather than a rate story. The TradingEconomics path does open later - 0.25% in Q1/27 rising to 0.75% by Q3/27 - and the SNB repeated it stands ready to intervene in FX, which is the ceiling on any disorderly franc rally. Swiss CPI is 1.0% with core 0.5%, the lowest on the board.

today.headline: Sterling sat still at 1.34108 and plus 0.03%, which is the right behaviour two days before the decision that is 94% priced.
today.read: The pound keeps the board outright and it is the one top-of-board case on this file that depends on neither the oil premium nor the AI trade. Thursday at 12:00Z the MPC is expected to take Bank Rate to 4.00% from 3.75%, with ForexFactory forecasting a 7-0-2 vote against September's 3-0-6 hold - a swing of four members. The domestic evidence supports it: CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 and wage growth 3.7%, and the September minutes already said further CPI increases are expected in coming quarters. The reason to own the hike rather than sell it is the path: TradingEconomics carries 4.00% in Q4/26 then 4.25% from Q1/27. The invalidation is specific and arrives the same hour - a Monetary Policy Report that pushes back on bets for several more increases, and Bailey at 12:30Z.

today.headline: The euro was unchanged at 1.11920 and plus 0.04%, holding a December hike that is priced between 82% and 94% with nothing on the calendar until the 17th.
today.read: The ECB held the deposit facility at 2.50% on October 29 with the refi rate at 2.65%, and the single most useful detail is that Lagarde confirmed the Governing Council discussed a hike before agreeing unanimously to hold. September HICP was 3.8%, up from 3.2%, with core at 2.5%. The statement's framing is a two-sided one that will matter if the AI trade keeps deteriorating: elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity, and underlying inflation is broadly stable with no significant wage response - negotiated wage growth is just 2.44%. The euro-specific energy problem is gas rather than crude, and it is getting worse not better: EU gas is 95.92 EUR/MWh and plus 30.48% on the month even as Brent fell 3.33% on the week. France's fiscal and political situation remains the live spread risk. October flash HICP lands Wednesday.

today.headline: USD/JPY was flat at 157.835 and minus 0.07% through a global equity correction, which is the third time in a week the yen has refused a haven bid.
today.read: Nothing moved and that is the information. A technical correction in the Nasdaq 100, a liquidation in gold and a ten-point fall in December Fed pricing are, between them, as clean a set of yen tailwinds as this market offers, and the pair did not break 157. What is holding it under 158 is not demand for yen but Finance Minister Katayama, who has said the joint FX statement with the United States still stands and that Tokyo is prepared to act against excessive or disorderly weakness. The forward case remains genuinely strong and this file is not abandoning it: the BoJ held 1.25% on October 30 by 8-1 with Takata dissenting for an immediate 1.5%, the Bank lifted its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4%, Ueda told parliament underlying inflation is quite close to target, and December 18 is priced at 75% to 80%. But a thesis spot has declined three times is one to express against the franc rather than against the dollar. Ueda speaks Friday at 16:00Z.

USD.when: December 9, with new Economic Projections and no November meeting
USD.note: Held at a 4.00% upper bound on October 28 by a 10-2 vote, with two policymakers preferring a quarter point, and Chair Warsh declined to commit to December. TradingEconomics forecasts 4.25% in Q4/26. Market pricing has deteriorated materially this week: CME FedWatch now reads roughly 71% to 74% against about 80% a week ago, and the reason given is the AI investment slowdown rather than anything in the inflation data, which remains hot at 3.7% CPI and 6.3% PPI. Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast is the resolution.

EUR.when: December 17, the final 2026 meeting on the ECB calendar
EUR.note: Deposit facility held at 2.50% on October 29 with the refi rate at 2.65%, and Lagarde confirmed at the press conference that the Governing Council discussed a hike before agreeing unanimously to hold. The statement warned that elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity if indirect and second-round effects intensify, but said underlying inflation is broadly stable with no significant wage response so far - negotiated wage growth is 2.44%. Trackers price December between 82% and 94% depending on source and date. HICP was 3.8% in September with core 2.5%.

GBP.when: November 5 at 12:00Z, with the Monetary Policy Report and Bailey at 12:30Z
GBP.note: Bank Rate has been 3.75% since the September 16 meeting, where the MPC voted 6-3 to hold with Pill, Greene and Mann preferring 4.00%, the same split as July. ForexFactory forecasts a 7-0-2 vote this week, pricing runs 93.5% to 94% and ING argues high energy prices leave the Bank no alternative. TradingEconomics carries 4.00% in Q4/26 then 4.25% from Q1/27, so this is the first of two rather than a terminal move. The risk is a Report that caps the path at 4.00%.

JPY.when: December 18, with Ueda speaking Friday November 6 at 16:00Z before then
JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 by an 8-1 vote, Takata dissenting for an immediate move to 1.5%, after consecutive 25bp hikes in June and September took the rate to its highest since April 1995. The quarterly outlook kept FY2026 inflation at 2.5% and lifted FY2027 to 2.6% from 2.4%. Ueda told parliament underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and that failing to adjust could stoke an overshoot. Swaps imply 75% to 80% for December. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50%.

AUD.when: December 8 at 03:30Z, with the minutes November 17
AUD.note: Hiked 25bp to 4.85% this morning on a 6-3 majority, three members preferring a hold, the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods, and sees inflation above 3% over the coming year. Bullock then gave no forward guidance at all. That combination - top rate on the board, no direction, and an AI demand leg that copper is now questioning - reads as a pause into February.

NZD.when: December 9, with a full Monetary Policy Statement - now genuinely two-sided
NZD.note: Still the base case but weaker than it was this morning. Q3 labour data on November 3 missed on every measure: unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against plus 0.4%, Q2 revised down to plus 0.3% from plus 0.5%, participation 70.4% from 70.6% and private-sector wages ex overtime 2.0% year over year from 2.1%. That is the opposite of the repair this file was waiting for. Against it: the October 28 hold was 4-3 with members agreeing further tightening would likely be needed, Governor Breman said afterwards the chance of a December hike is high, the RBNZ forecasts 4.4% inflation in December with fuel pass-through still to come, and TradingEconomics keeps 3.00% for December and the steepest path on this board toward 4.00% by Q3/27. Westpac still forecasts a December hike but now calls it not a done deal. Pricing ran 77% to 80% before the print; a verified post-print number is not yet available. Watch front-end swaps rather than spot.

CAD.when: December 9, but closer to a coin flip than a base case
CAD.note: Hiked 25bp to 2.50% on October 28, the first increase in three years, to reduce the risk that high energy prices spread into broader goods and services, while saying caution is necessary. The Bank sees CPI averaging 3% in 2027, a full point above the July projection, and growth of 1% in 2026 then 2% in 2027 and 2028. Macklem said there is no predetermined path. Crude bouncing today supports the case; September employment at minus 68,300 and Friday's print against a plus 14.6k forecast are the counterweight.

CHF.when: December 10, with the Quarterly Bulletin December 16
CHF.note: Held at 0.00% on September 24, unchanged since mid-2025, with the SNB saying the stance remains appropriate and repeating that it is willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary. Inflation has risen to 1.0% from 0.8% in August on energy, and the Bank expects a further rise in the fourth quarter before easing through 2027, forecasting 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for 2027 and 2028. The TradingEconomics path has 0.00% in Q4/26 then 0.25% in Q1/27 and 0.75% by Q3/27, so the franc is not permanently capped - just not moving this quarter.

The Bank hiked on October 28 to stop high energy prices spreading into broader goods and services and projects CPI averaging 3% in 2027, a full point above July, but Macklem said there is no predetermined path and National Bank put December near 50%. Core at 2.2% is the softest on this board outside Switzerland and Japan, and new US tariffs follow the breakdown of trade talks. Friday's employment print at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast is the single biggest input into December 9.

strength.tag: Top rate, no guidance, falling copper
strength.drivers: The cash rate at 4.85% after a 6-3 hike, the highest since late 2008, with CPI 4.3% and core 3.6%, against September employment at minus 39,300, unemployment at 4.7% and rising, GDP at 2.1% and AUD/USD at 0.69805 and minus 0.27%.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Holds the highest policy rate on this board and has lost the directional case for it: Bullock delivered the fifth hike of the year and then declined to guide at all. What is new today is a second crack. The statement named AI-related demand for technology goods as a source of broad-based price pressure alongside fuel and capacity constraints, and copper - the market's cleanest read on that demand - is 6.3646 and minus 2.73%, minus 3.96% on the week. So the inflation case the RBA just acted on is being questioned by the commodity most tied to Australia. The domestic data points the same way. December 8 reads as a hold and February is the meeting to trade; the minutes land November 17. A copper recovery would restore the hawkish leg quickly.

strength.drivers: DXY at 101.739 and minus 0.04%, the funds rate held at a 4.00% upper bound by a 10-2 vote with two dissents for a hike, CPI 3.7% and PPI 6.3% year over year, with September payrolls at 29,000 and unemployment at 4.2%.
strength.forward: ⚖️ The data is hawkish and the pricing is not, and the gap opened this week rather than today. December 9 has fallen to roughly 71% to 74% from about 80% a week ago, and the reason analysts give is the AI investment slowdown rather than anything in the inflation prints, which remain the hottest on this board. The committee's hawkish wing is intact - two members voted to hike in October - so this is a market losing confidence that growth permits the move, not a Fed changing its mind. Two dated resolutions: today's midterms at 15:16Z, where a Democratic sweep at 74% to 78% has hardened enough that the move now lives in the tail rather than the base case, and Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast. A strong print rebuilds December and the dollar with it.

strength.drivers: Q3 unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast and the highest since 2016, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against plus 0.4% with Q2 revised to plus 0.3%, participation 70.4% from 70.6% and private wages 2.0% year over year; NZD/USD 0.55857 and minus 0.52%, OCR 2.75% after a 4-3 hold, CPI 3.7% with core 3.2%.
strength.forward: 🔻 Downgraded from minus 1 on a dated test this file set itself. The case for keeping the kiwi only one notch below the pack was that its path is the steepest on this board and that two near-dated events could repair the timing discount; the first of those has now failed on every measure, including a downward revision to the quarter before. The forward path is not dead - the October hold was 4-3 with members agreeing further tightening would likely be needed, Governor Breman said afterwards the chance of a December hike is high, the RBNZ still forecasts 4.4% inflation in December with fuel pass-through to come, and TradingEconomics keeps 3.00% for December and 4.00% by Q3/27 - but a labour market loosening while wage growth slows to 2.0% is the wrong input into that path, and Westpac now calls December not a done deal. Pricing was 77% to 80% before the print; no verified post-print figure yet. Invalidation is specific: a hawkish RBNZ Financial Stability Report on November 10, or front-end swaps holding their December pricing despite this, would say the market is looking through the labour data to fuel-driven CPI. Saturday's election is the last scheduled repair point.

symbols.why: A one-point gap at 1.11920 and plus 0.04%: the euro carries a December hike priced 82% to 94% after Lagarde confirmed the Council discussed hiking, against a dollar whose own December has slipped from about 80% to roughly 72% on the AI scare.
symbols.risk: The dollar leg votes today at 15:16Z before the euro leg has any catalyst, which is a sizing problem rather than a direction problem - keep it small. Wednesday's October flash HICP is a medium folder so it moves spot without a scheduled window, and EU gas at plus 30.48% on the month is a euro-area growth tax the ECB itself flagged.

symbols.why: The two-point gap and the cleanest near-dated catalyst on the board: Thursday 12:00Z is 93.5% to 94% priced for 4.00% on a forecast 7-0-2 vote, with the TE path extending to 4.25% from Q1/27, against a dollar losing December probability.
symbols.risk: The Monetary Policy Report lands the same minute as the decision and Reuters has flagged the Bank may use it to push back on bets for several more increases; Bailey follows at 12:30Z. A capped path takes this straight back to MEDIUM. Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast is the dollar-side risk.

symbols.why: Scores a one-point gap and the BoJ is 75% to 80% priced for December 18 after Takata dissented for an immediate 1.5%, but at 157.835 and minus 0.07% the pair refused to break 157 through an equity correction and a gold liquidation.
symbols.risk: Downgraded in sizing rather than direction, because the thesis has failed three times in a week. What holds the pair under 158 is Katayama's intervention warning, not yen demand, and a strong payroll on Friday sends it to 159. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z. CHF/JPY is the cleaner expression of the same view.

symbols.why: At 1.39701 and minus 0.12% with WTI at 97.301 and plus 0.87%, the currency has begun to follow the crude move this file flagged yesterday as missing, and core CPI at 2.2% plus a hike already delivered keeps Canada at plus one.
symbols.risk: December 9 is a coin flip rather than a base case - Macklem says there is no predetermined path and National Bank put it near 50%. Friday's employment at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast, after minus 68,300, is the real test, and new US tariffs follow the breakdown of trade talks. Oil remains a two-way headline binary.

symbols.why: Two currencies losing their forward case at once: the RBA delivered 4.85% and no guidance while copper fell 2.73%, and the dollar lost ten points of December probability. At 0.69805 and minus 0.27% there is no directional edge.
symbols.risk: Trade the levels, not the story. Today's midterms at 15:16Z and Friday's payrolls can resolve the dollar leg in either direction inside one session, and a copper recovery would restore the Australian leg just as fast. The RBA minutes on November 17 are the next scheduled read.

symbols.why: The first of the kiwi's two repair points failed: Q3 unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast, employment minus 0.1% against plus 0.4% and Q2 revised to plus 0.3%, with participation down to 70.4% and private wages at 2.0% year over year. Spot is 0.55857 and minus 0.52%, minus 1.69% on the week, and the score moves to minus 2.
symbols.risk: The dollar leg is the weak half of this ticket, not the kiwi one: December Fed pricing has slipped to roughly 71% to 74% on the AI-capex scare and Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast could cut either way, which is why this stays MEDIUM. On the kiwi side the remaining repair is Saturday's election, and front-end swaps holding their December pricing through this print would say the market is looking through the labour data.

symbols.why: At 0.81802 and minus 1.51% on the month, this is the cleanest expression of the franc upgrade: through an equity correction that liquidated gold, the franc gained on the dollar while the dollar's own December hike pricing fell from about 80% to roughly 72%.
symbols.risk: The SNB is at 0.00% and has said explicitly it remains willing to intervene in FX as necessary, which caps a disorderly rally. A strong payroll on Friday rebuilds the dollar leg, and a US-Iran breakthrough would remove the haven bid outright. Swiss CPI at 1.0% gives the SNB no reason to help.

symbols.why: Two plus-one currencies with hikes priced on consecutive December dates - the ECB on the 17th at 82% to 94%, the BoJ on the 18th at 75% to 80% - leaves no score gap at 176.664 and minus 0.02%.
symbols.risk: This is a levels trade with two scheduled resolutions nine hours apart in December. Nearer term, Japanese intervention risk truncates the downside while EU gas at plus 30.48% on the month truncates the upside. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z and Wednesday brings euro-area flash HICP.

symbols.why: Both at plus one and both with a damaged forward leg: the ECB discussed a hike and held, the RBA hiked and refused to guide. At 1.60324 and plus 0.30%, with the pair plus 1.24% on the week, the euro is winning the argument slowly.
symbols.risk: A copper recovery restores the Australian side quickly, since the RBA's own statement leans on AI-related technology demand that copper is currently repricing. On the euro side, French fiscal risk and a soft Wednesday flash HICP both cut the other way. No score gap means no size.

symbols.why: A three-point gap now the kiwi is at minus 2, and the trade has delivered: the cross broke the 2.00 handle on the Q3 labour miss and trades 2.00305 and plus 0.56%, plus 2.08% on the week. The euro holds the most certain December hike on this board after Lagarde confirmed the Council debated hiking; New Zealand's labour market just loosened to 5.7% unemployment with wage growth at 2.0%.
symbols.risk: The round number cuts both ways now it has been taken - a failure back under 2.00 would be the signal the move is done. Saturday's New Zealand election is the one remaining kiwi repair point. On the euro side Wednesday's October flash HICP is the near-dated test of a December hike priced between 82% and 94%.

symbols.why: The one-point gap runs the other way at 0.83465 and minus 1.67% on the month: sterling has the nearer catalyst on Thursday at 93.5% to 94% priced and the longer path to 4.25%, while the euro waits until December 17.
symbols.risk: This is a pure Thursday trade and it resolves inside thirty minutes. A Monetary Policy Report that caps Bank Rate at 4.00%, or Bailey pushing back at 12:30Z, reverses it immediately. Wednesday's euro-area flash HICP comes first and a 4-handle would narrow the gap from the other side.

symbols.why: Two plus-one currencies at 1.56361 and minus 0.07%, with the pair minus 2.30% on the month as the loonie firmed. The euro's December is near-certain and Canada's is a coin flip, but Canada has already hiked and the euro has not.
symbols.risk: Crude is the swing factor and it is a two-way headline binary while the Hormuz plan waits on Washington. Friday's Canadian employment at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast is the dated risk, and a second weak print after minus 68,300 would open this to the upside.

symbols.why: At 0.91563, minus 0.73% on the week and minus 1.77% on the month, the franc has been winning this cross steadily through the de-risking episode, and the euro area is the one carrying a 30.48% monthly rise in gas prices as a growth tax.
symbols.risk: Both legs score plus one, so this is a trend trade rather than a gap trade - keep it small. The SNB has said it remains willing to intervene in FX, which is an explicit cap, and a hawkish Wednesday flash HICP would put the euro leg back on top. The ECB's December hike is far more certain than anything the SNB will do.

symbols.why: A one-point gap where the sterling leg has a dated 94%-priced catalyst on Thursday and the yen leg keeps failing in spot. At 211.669 and plus 1.38% on the month.
symbols.risk: The yen's forward case is genuinely strong for December 18 at 75% to 80%, so this is a two-week trade rather than a two-month one, and Japanese intervention risk cuts hardest in exactly this kind of high-beta cross. A Monetary Policy Report that caps the UK path removes the near leg. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z.

symbols.why: A one-point gap at 1.92088 and plus 0.28%, plus 1.42% on the week: sterling has a hike arriving Thursday with a path beyond it, while Australia has the board's highest rate, no guidance and copper falling beneath its stated inflation case.
symbols.risk: Australia is not weak - 4.85% is the top of this board and CPI is 4.3% - so this is a forward-guidance trade, not a fundamentals trade. A copper recovery or a hawkish set of RBA minutes on November 17 would close the gap, and a capped UK path on Thursday removes the other leg.

symbols.why: A four-point gap and the widest on the board now the kiwi is minus 2 against sterling's plus 2. At 2.40157 and plus 0.70%, plus 2.45% on the week, after New Zealand's Q3 labour data missed on every measure - unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast, employment minus 0.1% against plus 0.4% - while the Bank of England is 93.5% to 94% priced to hike Thursday at 12:00Z on a 7-0-2 vote forecast.
symbols.risk: One of the two binaries is now behind it, which raises the conviction and concentrates the remaining risk in sterling: a Monetary Policy Report that caps Bank Rate at 4.00%, or Bailey at 12:30Z pushing back, removes the strong leg in one hour on Thursday. Saturday's New Zealand election is the kiwi-side repair. The cross is extended, so levels matter more than they did this morning.

symbols.why: A one-point gap at 1.87336 and minus 0.09%, but the cheapest version of the sterling trade because the Canadian leg is improving: crude bounced 0.87% today and the loonie followed, which is what this file said was missing yesterday.
symbols.risk: Two employment prints and one rate decision sit between here and resolution. Friday's Canadian jobs at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast prints the same minute as US payrolls, so the cross can gap on an input that has nothing to do with sterling. Oil remains a two-way headline binary.

symbols.why: A one-point gap at 1.09702 and minus 0.07%, where sterling's Thursday catalyst meets the one currency that is genuinely bid on the de-risking - which is why this is the weakest of the five sterling longs rather than the strongest.
symbols.risk: If the AI-capex scare deepens, the franc leg strengthens faster than the sterling leg can price a hike that is already 94% in. The SNB's intervention pledge is the only thing capping the franc. A capped UK path on Thursday leaves this exposed to a pure haven bid.

symbols.why: Two plus-one currencies, both of which lost something this week: the RBA hiked to 4.85% and refused to guide, the yen refused a haven bid for the third time. At 110.1810 and minus 0.33%.
symbols.risk: This is the board's highest-beta risk proxy and it sits directly under the AI story - a deeper Nasdaq correction hits both legs, the Australian one through copper and the yen one through carry unwind, which is why it ranges rather than trends. Japanese intervention risk truncates the upside near 158 on the dollar cross.

symbols.why: A three-point gap: Australia holds 4.85% after a 6-3 hike, the highest since late 2008, while New Zealand's Q3 labour market loosened to 5.7% unemployment with employment minus 0.1% and wages at 2.0%. At 1.24672 and plus 0.03%, having turned higher on the print after being minus 0.47% earlier in the session - the entry this file flagged yesterday held.
symbols.risk: Australia's own labour market is also deteriorating - September employment minus 39,300 with unemployment at 4.7% and rising - and Bullock gave no guidance at all, so the Australian leg is a rate level rather than a direction. Falling copper, minus 3.96% on the week, undercuts the AI leg of the RBA's inflation case and hurts the Australian side more. Saturday's New Zealand election is the kiwi repair point; the RBA minutes land November 17.

symbols.why: Both at plus one and both commodity currencies whose commodities are moving in opposite directions: crude is plus 0.87% and copper minus 2.73%. At 0.97523 and minus 0.38%, minus 1.90% on the month, Canada is winning that exchange.
symbols.risk: Trade the levels. Friday's Canadian employment at 13:30Z is the one dated event that can break the range, and a second weak print after minus 68,300 would flip the commodity advantage back. The RBA minutes on November 17 are the Australian-side read.

symbols.why: At 0.57110, minus 0.34% today and minus 1.95% on the week, this is the cleanest pairing of the day's two themes: the franc is bid on the de-risking while the Australian dollar's inflation case leans on an AI demand impulse that copper is actively repricing.
symbols.risk: Both legs score plus one, so size it as a trend trade. Australia holds the highest policy rate on the board at 4.85% with CPI at 4.3%, which is real support, and the SNB's stated willingness to intervene caps the franc. A copper recovery reverses this quickly.

symbols.why: A three-point gap on paper after the kiwi's downgrade - New Zealand's Q3 unemployment at 5.7% and employment minus 0.1% against a BoJ board that held 1.25% 8-1 with Takata dissenting for 1.5% and December 18 priced 75% to 80% - but the cross is only 88.6560 and minus 0.03%, because the yen is weakening too.
symbols.risk: This is the clearest case on the board of a wide fundamental gap that spot will not pay: USD/JPY has now pushed through 158 to 158.714 and plus 0.49%, so the yen leg that should amplify this trade is failing for a fourth time. Stays MEDIUM, and the kiwi weakness is better expressed against the euro, sterling or the franc. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z; Saturday is the New Zealand election.

symbols.why: A three-point gap at 0.78254 and minus 0.36%, minus 1.90% on the week: Canada has already delivered its hike to 2.50% and has crude at 97.301 and plus 0.87% behind it, while New Zealand's Q3 labour data loosened on every measure - unemployment 5.7%, employment minus 0.1%, wages 2.0% - and left its December hike two-sided.
symbols.risk: The kiwi leg is now settled until Saturday's election and the open risk has shifted entirely to Canada: employment Friday at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast after September's minus 68,300, with December 9 near a coin flip on National Bank's read and core inflation at 2.2%, the softest here outside Switzerland and Japan. A weak Canadian print stalls this; a Hormuz reopening removes the crude support.

symbols.why: A three-point gap at 0.45854 and minus 0.27%, minus 2.56% on the week: the board's weakest currency, downgraded to minus 2 after Q3 unemployment printed 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast with employment minus 0.1%, against the one haven that actually worked through the equity correction and the gold liquidation.
symbols.risk: The franc leg is a relative-safety bid rather than a rate story - the SNB is at 0.00%, December 10 is a hold and the Bank has said it stands ready to intervene in FX - so a US-Iran breakthrough together with an AI-capex recovery would remove it. Stays MEDIUM for that reason. Saturday's New Zealand election is the last scheduled kiwi repair point before December 9.

symbols.why: Two plus-one currencies at 112.9790 and plus 0.05%, with the pair plus 2.03% on the month as crude held up and the yen did not. No score gap, and both legs face December decisions that are live rather than settled.
symbols.risk: Trade the levels. The Bank of Canada's December 9 is near a coin flip while the BoJ's December 18 is 75% to 80% priced, so the risk is skewed to the downside if Canadian jobs disappoint Friday at 13:30Z. Japanese intervention risk caps the upside.

symbols.why: Both at plus one and this is the one franc cross the franc has not been winning: 0.58556 and plus 0.02% today, plus 0.54% on the month, because crude strength has offset the haven bid.
symbols.risk: A two-way commodity binary against a haven bid - trade the levels. Friday's Canadian employment at 13:30Z is the dated risk and a second weak print would hand the cross to the franc. A Hormuz breakthrough would hit both legs at once, crude first.

symbols.why: The day's cleanest new idea: two havens, one of which worked. At 192.936 and plus 1.47% on the month, the franc gained through the Nasdaq correction and the gold liquidation while the yen refused a bid for the third time in a week.
symbols.risk: Both score plus one, so this is a behavioural trade rather than a rate trade, and the rate leg runs against it - the BoJ is 75% to 80% priced for December 18 while the SNB holds at 0.00% on December 10. Japanese intervention would hit this cross hard and fast. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z.

symbols.why: At 101.739 and minus 0.04%, holding near 102 while the December hike that underwrites it fell from about 80% to roughly 72%. With EUR at 57.6% of the basket and the euro's own hike near-certain, the index has no clean direction into a vote.
symbols.risk: Two dated binaries this week resolve it. Today's midterms at 15:16Z with a Democratic sweep at 74% to 78% means the base case is priced and the move lives in the tail; Friday's payrolls at a 65,000 forecast after 29,000 is the data that rebuilds or breaks December.

symbols.why: The yen is MIXED rather than strengthening, so the basket ranges: a December hike priced 75% to 80% on one side, and spot that would not break 157 through an equity correction on the other.
symbols.risk: This is the opposite ticket to every XXX/JPY pair here, so it inherits the same intervention asymmetry in reverse - Katayama's warning means the basket's upside is official rather than organic. Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z and December 18 is the decision.

symbols.why: At 25,782 and minus 0.77% today but plus 2.09% on the month and plus 7.65% on the year, the DAX is outperforming the EU50 by four points on the month because its industrials, autos and travel names benefit from cheaper crude.
symbols.risk: The leg that caps it is gas, not oil: Germany pays EUR gas at 96.22 EUR/MWh, plus 29.20% on the month, even as Brent fell 3.33% on the week, so the energy tailwind is narrower than the crude move suggests. A near-certain December ECB hike and the AI correction hitting Infineon and SAP are the other two headwinds.

symbols.why: At 6,120, minus 0.95% today and minus 1.95% on the month against the DAX at plus 2.09%, the index is being dominated by its AI-exposed heavyweights and French political risk rather than by the bank leg a hawkish ECB would help.
symbols.risk: The bank leg is the reason this is LOW-MED and not MEDIUM: banks are the heaviest sector here and a December ECB hike priced 82% to 94% with a steepening curve supports exactly that weight. Monday showed the other side, with the Stoxx 50 up nearly 1% on Iran peace hopes. A Hormuz deal would reverse this fast.

symbols.why: At 3920.33 and minus 0.68%, minus 5.30% on the month after the worst month since 2008, gold has two legs pulling opposite ways: forced liquidation out of the Nasdaq correction against a December Fed hike that has fallen from about 80% to roughly 72%.
symbols.risk: Do not trade this as a haven - it has not behaved as one for a month. The liquidation leg dominates while equities keep falling, but the real-rate leg strengthens every time December pricing slips. Today's midterms at 15:16Z and Friday's payrolls can resolve the rate leg in one session each.

symbols.why: At 49.279, minus 2.71% today, minus 9.43% on the week and minus 19.29% on the month, silver is decoupling from gold to the downside - the ratio is 79.55 against 77.77 yesterday - because its industrial leg sits directly in the AI-capex repricing.
symbols.risk: Silver is still plus 4.49% on the year and a 19% monthly drawdown invites a violent bounce; it rose 2.87% as recently as yesterday's session. A dovish repricing of the Fed would lift both metals, and an AI-capex recovery would lift silver more than gold. Size for the volatility, not the conviction.

symbols.why: At 6.3646 USD per pound, minus 2.73% today and minus 3.96% on the week, copper is the cleanest market read on the AI demand impulse that is now being questioned - and the same impulse the RBA named in this morning's statement.
symbols.risk: Copper is still plus 12.01% on the year and the physical story has not changed - LME stocks, mine disruption and tariff front-running all remain supportive, so this is a demand-expectations trade rather than a supply one. Chinese PMIs are the input that can reverse it, and a recovery restores the Australian dollar's case at the same time.

symbols.why: At 97.301 and plus 0.87%, still plus 8.80% on the month and plus 69.46% on the year, WTI is a headline binary in both directions: Araghchi's two-day Hormuz plan waits on a US answer that has not come, and OPEC+ left December output unchanged.
symbols.risk: Both tails are live inside the same week. Acceptance of Iran's conditions - lifting July sanctions, restoring the June waivers, shrinking the US presence, releasing frozen funds - would take out the remaining premium fast; Trump has instead warned that US targets remain. Physical supply is still constrained while Hormuz flows are disrupted. Keep this consistent with CAD at plus one.

jobs.note: Q3 employment q/q; Q2 cut to +0.3%

rates.note: OCR, held Oct 28 on a 4-3 vote

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate, Rate Statement and Monetary Policy Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Hiked 25 basis points to 4.85% on a 6-3 majority against a 4.60% previous, in line with the forecast - the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods, and sees inflation above 3% over the coming year.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Press Conference with Governor Bullock (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Bullock declined to provide forward guidance and did not replace the tightening bias the statement dropped, which reads as a pause into February rather than a continuing cycle. AUD/USD is 0.69805 and minus 0.27%, unrecovered.

catalysts.event: United States: Congressional Elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: Kalshi and Polymarket put a Democratic sweep at 74% to 78%, up from roughly 71% yesterday, with the House at 94% safe and the Senate near 74%. The base case has hardened enough that the tradeable move now sits in the tail rather than the base case. Combined midterm-linked betting volume is reported above $1.4 billion.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released and missed on every measure, TradingEconomics-verified. Unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast and 5.6% previously, the highest since 2016; employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against plus 0.4% forecast, with Q2 revised down to plus 0.3% from plus 0.5%. Participation fell to 70.4% from 70.6% and private-sector wages ex overtime slowed to 2.0% year over year, so the rise in unemployment came despite people leaving the workforce. This was the first of two dated repair points for the weakest currency on the board and it broke: NZD/USD minus 0.52% to 0.55857, EUR/NZD through 2.00.

catalysts.event: Euro area: October flash HICP
catalysts.note: The near-dated test of the ECB's December hike, which prices between 82% and 94%. September headline was 3.8% from 3.2% with core at 2.5%. The ECB said underlying inflation is broadly stable with no significant wage response so far, and negotiated wage growth is 2.44%.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Official Bank Rate, MPC Vote, Monetary Policy Summary and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: The single biggest scheduled event on this board. Forecast 4.00% from 3.75%, priced 93.5% to 94%, with ForexFactory carrying a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold - a swing of four members. The Report is the risk: Reuters has flagged the Bank may use it to push back on bets for several more increases.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Governor Bailey speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: Thirty minutes after the decision, and the second half of the same trade. The question is whether he endorses the TradingEconomics path of 4.25% from Q1/27 or caps guidance at 4.00%. A capped path takes sterling off the top of this board.

catalysts.event: United States: Non-Farm Employment Change, Unemployment Rate and Average Hourly Earnings (red folder)
catalysts.note: Payrolls forecast at plus 65k from plus 29k, unemployment forecast unchanged at 4.2%, average hourly earnings forecast plus 0.3% from plus 0.1%. This is the data that rebuilds or breaks a December 9 hike now priced at roughly 71% to 74%, down from about 80% a week ago.

catalysts.event: Canada: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Employment forecast at plus 14.6k after September's minus 68,300, unemployment forecast unchanged at 6.5%. Prints the same minute as US payrolls, and is the single biggest input into a December 9 Bank of Canada decision that National Bank puts near a coin flip.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ Governor Ueda speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: The last scheduled Ueda appearance before December 18, which swaps price at 75% to 80%. He told parliament on October 30 that underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and that failing to adjust could stoke an overshoot - but he also named strong global AI demand as a source of price pressure, and that demand is now being repriced.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Parliamentary Elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: Labour has pledged to restore the RBNZ's dual employment mandate if elected. Westpac notes the December 9 meeting proceeds under the current single mandate whatever the result, so this is a February-and-beyond institutional risk rather than a December one - which narrows the discount without removing it.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Financial Stability Report
catalysts.note: Lands two days after the election and three days before the December decision window opens. Worth watching for any commentary on the mandate question or on the housing and rates outlook.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Meeting Minutes
catalysts.note: The first detailed read on the 6-3 split behind this morning's hike and on how seriously the three dissenters argued the downside case. The key question is how much weight the Board put on AI-related technology demand that copper is now repricing.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC Minutes
catalysts.note: The record of the October 28 meeting where two policymakers dissented for a hike and Chair Warsh declined to commit to December. The hawkish wing's reasoning matters more than usual now that market pricing has slipped to roughly 72%.

catalysts.event: United States: Fed Beige Book
catalysts.note: Regional anecdote on whether the AI capital-spending slowdown is showing up in real activity, two weeks before the December 9 decision.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts
catalysts.note: The account of the October 29 meeting, where Lagarde confirmed the Governing Council discussed a hike before agreeing unanimously to hold. How close that discussion came is the best available read on December 17.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate decision
catalysts.note: Reads as a hold after Bullock declined to guide this morning. February is the meeting the market is now trading.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.note: The dot plot meeting, and the resolution of the hike now priced at roughly 71% to 74%. There is no November FOMC, so Friday's payrolls and the November CPI are the only major inputs between now and then.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ decision with Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% from 2.75%. Proceeds under the current single mandate whatever Saturday's election delivers, per Westpac.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada decision and Rate Statement
catalysts.note: A genuine coin flip. TradingEconomics forecasts 2.5%, National Bank put it near 50%, and Macklem has said there is no predetermined path. Friday's employment print is the swing input.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB decision
catalysts.note: Forecast 0.00%, unchanged since mid-2025. The TradingEconomics path has 0.25% from Q1/27, so the franc's current bid is relative safety rather than rates.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision, the final 2026 meeting
catalysts.note: Priced between 82% and 94% for a 25bp move taking the deposit facility to 2.75%. Lagarde confirmed the Council discussed hiking in October before holding unanimously.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ decision and Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% from 1.25%; swaps imply 75% to 80%. Takata already dissented for an immediate move at the October meeting, and the Bank lifted its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6%.

catalysts.event: Iran, the United States and the Strait of Hormuz
catalysts.note: Araghchi's two-day plan - US measures on day one, the Strait reopening on day two - remains an Iranian offer conditioned on Washington accepting a long list of demands, and Washington has neither accepted nor rejected it publicly. Trump has warned that US targets remain. Reports that the US has indicated readiness are attributed to Al Jazeera and are not independently confirmed. Both tails stay live.

catalysts.event: The AI capital-spending repricing and the Nasdaq correction
catalysts.note: The Nasdaq 100 is more than 10% below its October 6 high in its third correction of 2026, on doubts about AI capex returns and the debt funding it. This is now the second correlated risk on this board: it liquidated gold, broke silver and copper, and has taken about ten points off December Fed pricing. Three of these eight central banks cited AI demand as a reason to tighten.

catalysts.event: Japanese FX intervention risk
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Katayama has said the joint FX statement with the United States still stands and that Tokyo is prepared to act against excessive or disorderly yen weakness. The zone that matters is 158 to 159 on USD/JPY, and it is what is currently holding the pair rather than any demand for yen.

catalysts.event: OPEC+ output policy and the European gas market
catalysts.note: OPEC+ left December output targets unchanged. European gas is the separate and worsening energy story: EU gas is 95.92 EUR/MWh and plus 30.48% on the month, German gas 96.22 and plus 29.20%, even as Brent fell 3.33% on the week. That is a euro-area growth tax the ECB named in its October statement.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz has now been closed long enough that the oil premium is a structural feature of this board rather than an event, and the question this week is whether it starts to unwind. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Qatari mediation compressed Tehran's original seven-day proposal to two: Washington carries out a package of measures on day one, the Strait reopens and shipping returns to normal on day two. The conditions attached are not small and have not moved - lifting the sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum collapsed in July, reinstating the oil waivers granted in June, reducing the US military presence in the region, recognising shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman, and releasing frozen Iranian funds. The nuclear file is reportedly not part of the package. Washington has neither accepted nor rejected it publicly; reports that the United States has indicated readiness to accept are attributed to Al Jazeera and are not independently confirmed, and this file will not trade them. Trump has warned that US targets remain. Crude has done what you would expect of an unresolved binary: more than 6% lower on Monday, then WTI back to 97.301 and plus 0.87% and Brent to 105.762 and plus 0.95% today, still plus 8.80% and plus 5.42% respectively on the month and plus 69.46% and plus 73.81% on the year. OPEC+ left December output unchanged, and the physical constraint has not changed at all - what has moved is the probability traders assign to it ending. The FX transmission runs through four channels and one of them is new. First, the direct terms-of-trade channel: Canada is the clean beneficiary and USD/CAD at 1.39701 and minus 0.12% has finally started to follow crude, which is the gap this file flagged yesterday. Second, the inflation channel, which is why four of these eight central banks are tightening at all - the Fed named geopolitical developments in its October statement, the ECB warned elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity, the BoE attributed the rise in UK CPI to 3.1% in August directly to Middle East conflict, and the RBA cited elevated fuel and commodity prices this morning. A genuine Hormuz reopening would pull the rug from all four paths at once, which is the single largest correlated risk on this board. Third, the gas channel, which is specific to Europe and is moving the wrong way for the euro: EU gas is 95.92 EUR/MWh and plus 30.48% on the month, German gas 96.22 and plus 29.20%, even while Brent fell on the week - so for the euro area the energy shock is intensifying as a growth tax at the same time the oil premium deflates. Fourth, and new this week, the risk-appetite channel is no longer dominated by the war at all. The Nasdaq 100's third correction of 2026 is a separate shock running in the opposite direction, and it is already doing to the rate complex what a Hormuz deal would do - gold liquidated to its worst month since 2008, silver minus 19.29%, copper minus 2.73%, and December Fed pricing down from about 80% to roughly 72%. The two shocks are not additive: one is inflationary and one is disinflationary, and the hawkish consensus on this board needs the first to keep outrunning the second. The honest read is that it currently is not, and that FX has not priced either - DXY is 101.739 and minus 0.04%. The franc is the one currency behaving as though both are real.
